overlapWith: flight: that page is lift and stall on a wing section at level 2; this one never looks at the wing's shape, only at how flap rate and speed change with a bird's size across real species.

title: Why leaves change colour
interaction: Watch one maple leaf from late summer into autumn on a calendar scrub: as the days shorten and the nights cool, the green pigment is broken down and pulled back into the tree, and the yellow and orange that were underneath all along show through; sunny days with cold nights brew red on top. Then force the weather: a warm, dull autumn gives yellow without red, and an early frost cuts the show short.
takeaway: The yellow was in the leaf all summer, hidden under the green; the tree takes the green back before letting the leaf go.
needsSource: none for the model (green pigment broken down as days shorten and cool, yellow pigments constant, red made on bright cool days, leaf colour mixed from the pigments); if the colour is mixed from measured pigment spectra, PhotochemCAD's spectra are freely downloadable but their licence must be checked
pitfall: Leaves do not make yellow in autumn: the yellow was already there, and only the red is made fresh. Cold does not cause the change by itself: the shortening days are the main trigger.
why: England KS1 statutory requirement, Seasonal changes: observe changes across the four seasons; and the most-asked autumn question. https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study
overlapWith: photosynthesis: that page is the green pigment at work; this one is the green being dismantled and what it leaves behind.

title: Why you shiver and sweat
interaction: Put a person in weather from snowy to scorching, resting or running, and watch a heat budget: the body makes heat all the time and loses it through the skin, and a thermostat in the brain keeps the core at one temperature by turning the skin pale or flushed, then shivering, then sweating. Push the weather past what sweat can carry away and the core creeps up.
takeaway: You are a heater set to one temperature: shivering turns the heat up and sweating carries it away, and the colour of your skin shows which way the thermostat is pushing.
needsSource: none: a one-node heat balance with resting heat near a hundred watts, shivering up to several times that, skin blood flow, and sweat cooling by evaporation up to a stated maximum, from textbook physiology
pitfall: Sweat only cools when it evaporates, so sweat dripping off on a humid day has done nothing yet. And feeling cold is not the core being cold: the skin reports first, which is what the thermostat acts on.
why: NGSS MS-LS1-8: skin receptors respond to temperature and send messages to the brain for immediate behaviour. https://nyssls.info/index.php/MS-LS1-8
overlapWith: homeostasis: that page holds blood sugar steady with insulin; this one holds temperature steady with shivering and sweat, the same feedback idea with no hormones and one control at a time.

title: How you breathe
interaction: Drag the diaphragm down and up on a cutaway chest and watch the ribs lift, the lungs swell and air flow in through a counter, with a bell jar and balloon beside it doing the same thing. Let go and set a slider for sleeping, walking or sprinting to see breaths per minute and the size of each breath change; then hold the breath and watch the carbon-dioxide bar climb until the urge to breathe wins.
takeaway: The lungs cannot suck: the diaphragm makes the chest bigger, which lowers the pressure inside, and the outside air pushes itself in.
needsSource: none: chest volume to pressure by Boyle's law, airflow proportional to the pressure difference, and breathing rates by activity from textbook physiology, all stated on the page
pitfall: Breathed-out air is not carbon dioxide: it still holds most of the oxygen that went in, which is why rescue breaths work. And the lungs are not muscles; the diaphragm and the rib muscles do the work.
why: England KS3 programme of study: the mechanism of breathing to move air in and out of the lungs, using a pressure model to explain the movement of gases. https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study
overlapWith: heart-circulation: that page shows oxygen levels in the blood as the heart pumps; this one is the pump for air, with nothing about the blood.

title: Where your food goes
interaction: Pick a mouthful (bread, apple, cheese or a sweet) and push it through the tube on a scrub bar: the mouth, stomach, small intestine and large intestine each take their real time on a clock, and the mouthful breaks into ever smaller pieces only where the right juices are. Watch nutrient dots cross into the blood all along the coiled small intestine and what is left become waste; swap the food to see fat linger in the stomach and fibre pass through untouched.
takeaway: Food does not just fall through you: each part of the tube takes its own time and does its own job, and almost everything useful is taken out in the long, coiled small intestine.
needsSource: none: transit times and which juices act where are textbook physiology; the compartment model with first-order breakdown of starch, protein and fat is a stated simplification
pitfall: The stomach does not do most of digestion: it is a mixing bag of acid, and most breakdown and nearly all absorption happen in the small intestine. Food does not drop by gravity either; muscles squeeze it along, which is why you can swallow upside down.
why: England KS2 Year 4 statutory requirement: describe the simple functions of the basic parts of the digestive system in humans. https://www-legacy.stem.org.uk/resources/community/collection/12365/year-4-animals-including-humans
overlapWith: homeostasis: homeostasis plots blood sugar after a meal has been absorbed; this page is the tube itself, what happens to the mouthful before anything reaches the blood.

title: What a fever is
interaction: Catch a germ and step through a fever: the brain turns the thermostat up to 39 degrees, so a body at its normal temperature now reads as too cold, shivers and curls under a blanket until it reaches the new setting; when the germ is beaten the setting drops back and the same body reads as too hot and sweats. Drag the thermostat yourself to see the chills come from raising it and the sweats from lowering it.
takeaway: A fever is not the body overheating: the brain raises its own thermostat, which is why you shiver on the way up and sweat on the way down.
needsSource: none: the body-thermostat heat model with a moving set point
pitfall: A fever is a setting the body chooses, not a fault in its heating; a fever-reducing medicine lowers the setting, it does not cool the body. The page does not claim that the heat kills germs.
why: NGSS MS-LS1-8: skin receptors respond to temperature; the fever page is the thermostat page's own example and the most-asked question about being ill. https://nyssls.info/index.php/MS-LS1-8
overlapWith: homeostasis: that page breaks a feedback loop to model diabetes; this one moves the loop's target on purpose and watches the body chase it.

title: Germs and hand washing
interaction: Watch a classroom through a morning under germ light: one child's hands glow, every door handle, pencil and hand they touch takes a share, and the next hand to touch the handle takes a share of that, the counts shrinking with each hop and as germs die on dry surfaces. Choose who washes and when, with soap for a proper count or a quick rinse, and see how far the glow has got by lunchtime.
takeaway: Germs travel hand to thing to hand, losing a share at each hop, and one good wash cuts the chain.
needsSource: Transfer fractions per touch and surface die-off rates from published fomite-transmission studies (e.g. Rusin, Maxwell and Gerba 2002) stated on the page; no dataset shipped
pitfall: Germs on a dry doorknob do not multiply, they slowly die; the danger is the hop to a hand and from the hand to a mouth. Soap works mostly by lifting germs off so the water can carry them away, which is why the time spent rubbing matters.
why: England statutory RSHE and health education guidance, primary health education: personal hygiene and germs including bacteria, viruses, how they are spread and treated, and the importance of handwashing. https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/relationships-education-relationships-and-sex-education-rse-and-health-education
overlapWith: epidemics: that page spreads an infection through a moving crowd and plots the curves; this one is one classroom's hands and surfaces, counted, with no curves and no immunity.

title: How you grow
interaction: Slide a child's age from birth to twenty along real growth curves and watch the figure grow, with the typical range of heights shaded so that a tall nine-year-old and a short twelve-year-old are both normal; a second curve shows how much is added each year: a lot in the first year, a slow plateau, one last spurt, then nothing. Switch between girls and boys to see the spurt land at different ages.
takeaway: You do not grow steadily: fastest as a baby, slowly through childhood, one last spurt, and then growing stops for good.
needs: CDC Growth Charts data files (stature-for-age and weight-for-age percentiles, 2000; a US government work, public domain): https://www.cdc.gov/growthcharts/cdc-data-files.htm. Growth per year is derived by differencing the chart.
needsSource: CDC Growth Charts data files, US government work (public domain)
pitfall: Being below or above the middle line is not behind or ahead: the shaded band is normal, and the spurt's timing varies by years between children. The charts describe typical children, not a target.
why: England KS2 Year 5 statutory requirement: describe the changes as humans develop to old age. https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study
overlapWith: homeostasis: that page plots hours of one person's blood sugar; this one scrubs years of the typical child's height from a real dataset, the way deep-time scrubs its record.

title: How your ear hears
interaction: Slide a tone from low to high and watch it shake the eardrum, three tiny bones lever the shake into the fluid of the snail-shaped cochlea, and a ripple run along its ribbon until it peaks at one spot; each pitch peaks somewhere else, high notes near the entrance and low notes at the far end. Play two notes at once and see two bumps; turn the loudness up and the bumps grow.
takeaway: The ear sorts sounds by pitch before the brain hears them: each note makes a different place along the spiral wiggle.
needsSource: none: the Greenwood (1961) frequency-to-place function for the human cochlea, a middle-ear lever ratio, and a passive bank of tuned filters for the ribbon, stated as a simplification
pitfall: The cochlea is not a microphone with one signal: it is thousands of sensors each listening at its own spot. And loud is not the same as high: loudness grows the bump, pitch moves it.
why: NGSS MS-LS1-8: sensory receptors respond to stimuli, with ear receptors reacting to vibrations. https://nyssls.info/index.php/MS-LS1-8
overlapWith: waves-interference: that page is the wave in the air; this one is the receiver, from eardrum to the place-by-pitch map. The reserve item Hearing and the cochlea merges here at level 0; the cochlea's own mechanics (travelling wave, active amplifier) stay open for a level-3 page.

title: Your pulse
interaction: Put two fingers on your own wrist and count along with a pulse the page beats for you: a stopwatch counts fifteen seconds and multiplies by four. Then slide the figure from resting to walking to sprinting and watch the beat speed up and the push of each beat travel down the arm to the wrist; stop, and the rate drifts back down over a minute or two, faster for a fit heart.
takeaway: Your pulse is the heart's push arriving at your wrist, and it speeds up with effort because working muscles need more blood.
needsSource: none: heart rate rising with effort toward a maximum near 220 minus age, recovery as an exponential with a fitness-dependent time, and the pulse as a pressure wave travelling far faster than the blood, from textbook physiology
pitfall: The pulse is not the blood arriving: the push travels along the artery many times faster than the blood itself moves. And a slower resting pulse usually means a stronger heart, not a weaker one.
why: England KS2 Year 6: the circulatory system and the effect of exercise, taught by measuring the pulse before and after two minutes of exercise. https://www-legacy.stem.org.uk/resources/community/collection/13109/year-6-animals-including-humans
overlapWith: heart-circulation: that page is inside the heart, with valves, an ECG and a pressure curve; this one never opens the heart: it is the beat you can feel and how exercise changes it.

title: How a broken bone mends
interaction: Break a bone in a cutaway leg, choose whether it is held still in a cast or keeps moving, and run the weeks: blood pools at the break, a soft rubbery callus bridges it, bone fills the callus in, and over months the lump is trimmed back toward the old shape. With too much movement the bridge never forms; with no load at all during the trimming the bone stays thin.
takeaway: A broken bone mends itself by first growing a bigger lump of new bone than it needs and then slowly trimming it back; the cast only holds the pieces still while it does.
needsSource: none: the stages and typical timings are textbook orthopaedics (Marsell and Einhorn 2011 review); the grid model of callus that turns to bone where it is held still, and is removed where it carries no load, is a stated simplification
pitfall: The cast does not heal anything, and bone does not mend like a glued stick: the repair is living tissue that keeps being reshaped for months, which is why a healed bone can end up as strong as before.
why: England KS3 programme of study: the structure and functions of the human skeleton. https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study
overlapWith: bridges-structures: that page loads a structure until a member fails; this one starts from the failure and watches a living member rebuild itself.

title: How a cut heals
interaction: Make a cut of chosen depth in a slice of skin and scrub the days: blood cells pour out, platelets stick to the torn edge and to each other, and a net of fibres traps cells until the flow stops; a scab hardens on top while new skin cells creep across underneath. Make the cut wider and the plug takes longer; pick the scab early and the gap reopens.
takeaway: Bleeding stops because sticky cells pile up from the edges of the hole until they plug it, and the scab is that plug dried out while new skin grows under it.
needsSource: none: a particle simulation of flow through a hole with sticking rules for platelets and a fibre net, then a grid of skin cells migrating across the gap; timings from textbook wound healing, stated as a simplification
pitfall: A scab is not the new skin and the body does not heal from the outside in: the new skin grows underneath, from the edges, and the scab falls off when it is done.
why: NGSS 4-LS1-1: plants and animals have internal and external structures that function to support survival, with skin named as an example structure. https://www2.cde.ca.gov/cacs/id/web/29023
overlapWith: heart-circulation: that page keeps the blood inside the vessels; this one is what blood does when it leaks out.

title: Why you feel full
interaction: Eat something, a glass of water, an apple, a bowl of porridge or a bag of crisps, and watch the stomach stretch and a fullness gauge rise; then let the clock run as the stomach squeezes its contents out into the gut, fast for water and slow for fat, and the gauge falls toward hungry. Compare a small snack with a big bowl of soup holding the same energy: the soup fills you more and for longer.
takeaway: You feel full when your stomach is stretched and hungry when it empties, so foods with the same energy can keep you full for very different times.
needsSource: Gastric-emptying half-times by food type (liquids in tens of minutes, solid meals in a couple of hours, fat slower) from published meal studies stated on the page; fullness from stomach volume plus a slow signal from the gut; no dataset shipped
pitfall: Fullness is not a calorie counter: the stomach measures stretch and the gut reports slowly, which is why a bag of crisps can leave you hungry and a bowl of soup does not. The page calls no food bad.
why: England KS2 Year 3 statutory requirement: identify that animals, including humans, need the right types and amount of nutrition. https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study
overlapWith: homeostasis: that page plots blood sugar and insulin after a meal; this one stops at the stomach and never looks at the blood.

title: Build a joint
interaction: Build an arm, then a leg, by choosing a joint for each junction from a palette of hinge, pivot, ball-and-socket and fixed; then try to touch your nose, scratch your back and turn a key. The skeleton moves exactly as far as its joints allow, so a hinge at the shoulder leaves the hand stuck in one plane and a ball at the knee buckles under the body.
takeaway: Joints come in a few shapes, hinges, pivots and ball-and-sockets, and the body uses the shape that fits each job.
needsSource: none: forward kinematics with each joint type's degrees of freedom and textbook ranges of motion
pitfall: The elbow is not the only joint in the forearm: turning your palm over is a separate pivot joint below it, so a hinge alone cannot explain what an arm does. Fixed joints (the skull) are joints too.
why: England KS2 Year 3 statutory requirement: identify that humans and some other animals have skeletons and muscles for support, protection and movement. https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study
overlapWith: bridges-structures: the only existing build page; it assembles a structure to carry loads, while this one assembles joints to reach places, with no forces.

title: Muscles pull in pairs
interaction: Drag the hand of a cutaway arm up and down: the biceps shortens and bulges to lift it and the triceps to lower it, and tugging either muscle alone shows it can only pull, never push. Hang a bag of shopping from the hand and watch how hard the biceps must pull, many times the bag's weight, because it grips the forearm so close to the elbow.
takeaway: A muscle can only pull, so every joint needs a pair that take turns, and the one that grips near the elbow must pull far harder than the weight in your hand.
needsSource: none: a two-link lever with real attachment distances (biceps a few centimetres from the elbow, the hand some thirty-five centimetres away) gives the force ratio
pitfall: Muscles never push; the opposite movement is always another muscle pulling. And a bigger muscle does not change the lever: it still pulls from the same place.
why: England KS3 programme of study: the function of muscles and examples of antagonistic muscles. https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study
overlapWith: bridges-structures: that page colours beams by tension and compression under a load; this one is a living lever with two pullers, and the load is a shopping bag.

title: Reflexes
interaction: Touch a hot pan on screen and watch two signals race along the body's wiring: one takes the short loop to the spinal cord and straight back to the arm muscle, the other carries on up to the brain; the hand is away before the ouch arrives, with both times on a clock. Then take the page's own reaction test, click when the colour changes, and see your time land far above the reflex's.
takeaway: A reflex is a shortcut through the spinal cord, which is why your hand is off the hot pan before you feel the pain.
needsSource: none: path lengths times textbook nerve conduction speeds (tens of metres per second for the fast fibres, with a short delay at each junction), and a reaction-time test measured in the browser
pitfall: The brain does not decide to pull the hand away; it finds out afterwards. And the reflex is not faster because its signal travels faster: it is faster because its path is shorter.
why: NGSS MS-LS1-8: sensory receptors send messages that result in immediate behaviour or memories, with the hot-handle example. https://nyssls.info/index.php/MS-LS1-8
overlapWith: neurons: that page is the spike itself, ions and myelin at level 2; this one shows no voltage, only paths and timings, and the reader's own reaction time.

title: Smell and taste
interaction: Build a smell: drag a molecule across a row of a dozen receptor locks and see which ones it fits, lighting a pattern; a different molecule lights a different pattern, and two together light a new one, so the nose tells smells apart by the pattern rather than by one lock each. Then eat a strawberry with the nose pinched and watch only the tongue's five basic tastes light up: most of what you call flavour vanishes.
takeaway: There is no sensor for each smell: a smell is the pattern of many sensors lit at once, and most of what you taste is really smell.
needsSource: The receptor matrix is a stated toy with real counts (about four hundred human odorant-receptor types, five basic tastes), after the combinatorial-code result of Malnic, Hirono, Sato and Buck (1999, Cell 96:713); if an open odorant-receptor response dataset is used to fill it, its licence must be checked
pitfall: The tongue map (sweet at the tip, bitter at the back) is a myth: every taste is sensed all over the tongue. And flavour is not a sixth taste; it is smell arriving through the back of the mouth.
why: NGSS MS-LS1-8: sensory receptors respond to stimuli, with tongue and nose receptors reacting to specific chemicals. https://thewonderofscience.com/msls18
overlapWith: vision-color: that page builds colour from three cone types; this one builds a smell from hundreds of receptors, the same pattern idea with a different sense and a pinched-nose test.

title: Sugar and your teeth
interaction: Place snacks and drinks on a day's timeline and run it: each sugary bite drops the mouth's acid meter into the red for about half an hour, and the enamel on a close-up tooth wears away only while the meter is there. Try one big bag of sweets at once against the same sweets spread through the day, then add brushing with fluoride toothpaste and watch the meter recover faster.
takeaway: Teeth are damaged by how often sugar arrives, not by how much: the same sweets spread through the day keep the mouth acid for hours.
needsSource: Stephan curve: the published plaque pH-after-sugar curve (Stephan 1944, Journal of Dental Research; summarised at https://www.dentalcare.com/en-us/ce-courses/ce713/stephan-curve) is used as the model's shape; no dataset is shipped
pitfall: Sugar does not dissolve teeth: the bacteria in plaque turn it into acid, and the acid does the damage below a mouth pH of about 5.5. Sugar-free does not mean acid-free: fizzy drinks are acid on their own.
why: England KS2 Year 4 statutory requirement: identify the different types of teeth in humans and their simple functions, taught with tooth-decay investigations. https://www-legacy.stem.org.uk/resources/community/collection/12365/year-4-animals-including-humans
overlapWith: acids-bases: that page is the chemistry of acids; this one is one acid attack you can schedule, on a tooth, with no chemistry shown.

title: Why bruises change colour
interaction: Bump a shin, lightly or hard, and watch blood leak from tiny broken vessels and pool under the skin; then scrub the days: the pool darkens as its oxygen goes, turns green as the red pigment is taken apart, then yellow, then fades as the pieces are carried off. A harder bump makes a bigger pool that takes longer to clear, and a colour key under the scrubber tells you roughly how old a bruise is.
takeaway: A bruise is blood trapped under the skin, and its changing colours are the body taking that blood apart piece by piece.
needsSource: none: haemoglobin to biliverdin to bilirubin as first-order conversions in a spreading pool, with the colour mixed from the three pigments; timings stated as ranges, since bruise ageing varies with size and person
pitfall: Bruises are not blood going bad, and the green and yellow are not signs of infection: the yellow is the same pigment that colours jaundice, and it is the normal end of the clean-up.
why: Demand: a standing reader question in the Ask Discover column. https://www.discovermagazine.com/ask-discover-39543
overlapWith: heart-circulation: that page keeps blood in the vessels; this one follows blood that got out, day by day, with no pump.

title: Why a shot protects you
interaction: Let a germ into a body and watch a race of counts: the germ doubles every few hours while the body's matching defenders start from a handful and take about a week to multiply, so you are ill before they win. Give the same body a shot first, a harmless lookalike of the germ, and run the race again: the defenders start in their thousands and the germ never gets going; add a second shot and see the head start grow.
takeaway: A shot is a practice run: the defenders are already made, so the real germ loses the race before it can multiply enough to make you ill.
needsSource: none: two growth curves with textbook timescales (a first response taking about a week, a second taking days; germ doubling times stated), after the standard primary and secondary antibody curves
pitfall: The shot does not contain the illness and does not make you a little sick to teach you: it is a lookalike, and feeling sore or warm afterward is the practice run itself.
why: England statutory RSHE and health education guidance, primary health education: the facts and scientific evidence relating to vaccination and immunisation, introduced when vaccinations are offered to pupils. https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/relationships-education-relationships-and-sex-education-rse-and-health-education
overlapWith: mrna-vaccines: that page follows the mRNA into a cell at level 2, and immune-system selects the matching cells; this one shows no cells, only the race of counts with and without a head start.

title: Why spinning makes you dizzy
interaction: Spin a head on a chair with a slider and watch the fluid in the ear's three rings lag behind, bending the little flap that tells the brain turning; keep spinning at a steady speed and the fluid catches up, so the feeling fades. Stop suddenly and the fluid keeps going, the flap bends the other way, and the brain reports turning in the opposite direction while the room stands still: that is dizzy.
takeaway: Your ears sense turning with a ring of fluid, and when you stop spinning the fluid keeps going, so you feel you are turning the other way.
needsSource: none: the torsion-pendulum model of the semicircular canal (fluid lag with a time constant of a few seconds, plus the brain's longer velocity storage), driven by the slider's turning speed
pitfall: Dizziness after spinning is not blood sloshing or the brain being overwhelmed by speed: the sensor is faithfully reporting a real movement of fluid that is no longer the head's movement.
why: Demand: a standing Life's Little Mysteries question. https://www.livescience.com/33828-spinning-dizzy.html
overlapWith: oscillations-resonance: that page drives a spring; this one is a sensor's lag, with the same inner ear as hearing-and-the-ear but a different organ in it.

title: Why you get sleepy
interaction: Set a bedtime and a wake-up time and run three days: a sleep-pressure tank fills while you are awake and drains while you sleep, and a body clock sets the hours when sleep comes easily; sleepiness is the gap between them. Skip a night and watch the tank overflow; nap in the afternoon and see tonight's sleep come later; a strip under the plot shows the night's cycles of light and deep sleep.
takeaway: Sleepiness is a pressure that builds all day and drains at night, gated by a clock that opens a window for it; when the two disagree you lie awake tired or nod off at noon.
needsSource: none: the two-process model (Borbely 1982; retrospective at https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9540767/) is an exponential sleep pressure and a daily rhythm with two thresholds; the night stages follow the standard ninety-minute cycle
pitfall: The page explains when you get sleepy, not why animals sleep at all, which is still an open question. And a weekend lie-in drains the tank but does not move the clock, which is why Monday feels like jet lag.
why: England statutory RSHE and health education guidance, primary health education: the importance of sufficient good quality sleep for health, the amount of sleep recommended for their age, and practical steps for improving sleep. https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/relationships-education-relationships-and-sex-education-rse-and-health-education
overlapWith: homeostasis: that page is a feedback loop around blood sugar over hours; this one is a pressure and a clock over days, with no hormones shown.

title: A year of weather, two places
interaction: Scrub through one real year of daily weather at a chosen station: each day a bar from the night's low to the afternoon's high and a drop for the rain, the 365 days drawn in a ring. Pick a second place (a desert, a rainy tropical coast, the Arctic, a foggy coast, a snowy interior) and its ring appears beside the first. Flip to the next year: the days are different every time, but the shape of each ring, the climate, comes back.
takeaway: Weather is what happens today and nobody can tell you a month ahead; climate is the shape of the whole year, different in each place and the same from year to year.
needs: Daily high, low and rain for a handful of US stations in contrasting climates (Phoenix for desert, Hilo for wet tropics, Utqiagvik for the Arctic, San Francisco for a coast, Minneapolis for a continental interior) from NOAA GHCN-Daily (https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/products/land-based-station/global-historical-climatology-network-daily); US stations are US Government data, public domain. Non-US stations in GHCN-Daily carry no clear licence, so the page uses US stations only.
needsSource: NOAA GHCN-Daily, US stations only (US Government data, public domain)
pitfall: One cold week does not disprove a warming climate and one hot day does not prove it: the page compares whole years, never single days.
why: NGSS 3-ESS2-1: 'Represent data in tables and graphical displays to describe typical weather conditions expected during a particular season' (https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/3-ess2-1-earths-systems); England KS1 geography, seasonal and daily weather patterns.
overlapWith: greenhouse-effect (level 1) runs emission scenarios to 2100; this page shows no trend and no model, only measured days, to separate weather from climate before any warming is discussed.

title: Waves at the beach
interaction: A cross-section of sea from deep water to the sand, with a rubber duck floating on it. Watch a wave pass: the duck bobs round in a small circle and ends up where it started, so the water does not travel with the wave. Drag the sea floor to make the beach steeper or gentler: as the water gets shallow the waves slow down, bunch together, grow taller and finally topple and break, far out on a gentle beach and right at the shore on a steep one.
takeaway: A wave carries its shape across the sea while the water only circles in place, and waves break where the water gets too shallow to carry them.
needsSource: none (water waves slowing with depth, growing as they slow, breaking when their height nears the depth; a tracer following the orbital motion)
pitfall: Beach waves are not made by the tide: they are made by wind far out at sea, and the water only rushes forward in the surf, not on the way in.
why: NOAA National Ocean Service, 'Why does the ocean have waves?' (https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/wavesinocean.html); NGSS 4-PS4-1 and England KS3 geography, coasts.
overlapWith: waves-interference (level 1) is a ripple tank of interference, harmonics and Doppler; this page has one wave, a sloping floor and a duck, and sun-earth-moon's tides are not waves.

title: Why clouds form, and why their bottoms are flat
interaction: Drag a bubble of air up from the warm ground: it swells and its thermometer drops about one degree for every hundred metres, which is also why it is colder on a mountain, until the invisible water it carries turns to droplets and the bubble turns white. Every bubble released from the same ground turns white at the same height, so the clouds have flat bottoms; make the day more humid and the cloud base drops, dry the air and clouds form higher or not at all. A last step blows the bubble over a mountain: it rains on the side facing the wind and the air comes down the far side dry.
takeaway: Rising air cools, and a cloud appears at exactly the height where the air gets cold enough for its water to condense, which is why cloud bottoms are flat and why mountains are cold.
needsSource: none (dry-adiabatic cooling of a parcel and the Magnus saturation formula, the standard textbook model)
pitfall: It is not colder on a mountain because it is farther from the Sun: a few kilometres make no difference to sunlight, and the air up there is cold because it has expanded. Clouds are not made of vapour and are not lighter than air: they are droplets falling so slowly that the rising air carries them.
why: UCAR Center for Science Education, 'Clouds and How They Form' (https://scied.ucar.edu/learning-zone/clouds/how-clouds-form); NGSS MS-ESS2-4 on the changes of state in the water cycle.
overlapWith: atmosphere-weather (level 2) shows global convection, pressure systems and fronts; this page follows one bubble of air and one cloud, with no Coriolis and no map.

title: The compass and Earth's magnetic poles
interaction: A globe with a magnet buried inside, its field drawn as lines looping from pole to pole. Drag a compass anywhere on the surface and its needle swings to lie along the local line: near the equator it lies flat along the ground, and near a magnetic pole it tries to point straight down and becomes useless. The magnetic pole sits hundreds of kilometres from the geographic one and drifts year by year, so from most places the needle misses true north by an angle the page measures as you move.
takeaway: A compass does not point at the North Pole: it lines up with Earth's magnetic field, which comes out of a magnetic pole hundreds of kilometres from the geographic one and dips into the ground as you go north.
needs: Earth's field from the World Magnetic Model WMM2025 coefficients, NOAA NCEI (https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/products/world-magnetic-model), US Government work stated as public domain; a tilted offset dipole is the documented fallback.
needsSource: World Magnetic Model WMM2025 coefficients (NOAA NCEI, public domain)
pitfall: The needle is not pulled toward the North Star or the geographic pole, and the magnetic pole is not a fixed place: it has moved hundreds of kilometres in a lifetime.
why: England KS3 physics, Magnetism: 'Earth's magnetism, compass and navigation' and KS2 Year 3 'describe magnets as having 2 poles' (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study).
overlapWith: electromagnetism (level 2) covers fields, induction and Maxwell; this page uses one magnet, one needle and a globe, and is the only one where a compass is navigated.

title: Dew, fog and the cold glass
interaction: A glass of iced water stands in a room: drag its temperature down and watch the air touching it, nothing, nothing, then at one particular temperature, the dew point, the glass mists over. Switch to a field at night and drag the night's temperature down: the grass gets wet at the same dew point, keep going and the air itself turns to fog, and if the dew point is below freezing you get frost instead. Make the day more humid and the dew point rises, so the dew comes sooner.
takeaway: Air carries an invisible amount of water, and the moment anything cools it past one particular temperature, the dew point, that water comes out as drops, mist or frost.
needsSource: none (saturation vapour pressure from the Magnus formula, relative humidity, frost point)
pitfall: The water on a cold glass does not leak through the glass: it comes out of the air. Fog is a cloud sitting on the ground, not smoke or steam.
why: England KS2 science, Year 4 States of matter: 'identify the part played by evaporation and condensation in the water cycle' (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study).
overlapWith: states-of-matter (level 1) shows condensation in a box of molecules under temperature and pressure; this page shows it on a glass, on grass and in the air, at one temperature the reader finds by hand.

title: Fossils and rock layers
interaction: Drop a shell, a leaf or a fish onto a sea floor and let mud and sand rain down year after year; add another creature later, and another, and switch the sea for land for a while. The layers pile up, squeeze, harden into rock, and the buried creatures turn to stone. Then cut the cliff: the oldest things lie deepest, and the stretch that was land leaves leaves above shells.
takeaway: Rock layers pile up from the bottom, so in an undisturbed cliff deeper means older, and the fossils in each layer are a snapshot of what lived there then.
needsSource: none (sedimentation and compaction through time, relative dating by superposition; optionally real fossil occurrences from the Paleobiology Database, CC BY 4.0)
pitfall: A fossil is not a bone that survived: it is rock that took the bone's place. And layers are not one per year like tree rings.
why: NGSS 4-ESS1-1: 'Identify evidence from patterns in rock formations and fossils in rock layers to support an explanation for changes in a landscape over time' (https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/4-ess1-1-earths-place-universe); England KS2 Year 3: 'describe in simple terms how fossils are formed when things that have lived are trapped within rock'.
overlapWith: deep-time (level 1) scrubs a dated timeline of 4.5 billion years; this page has no dates at all, only the order of layers and what is buried in them.

title: Heat from underground
interaction: Drill a well down from a field and read the thermometer as it goes: the rock gets warmer with every kilometre, warm enough for a bath a few kilometres down and for steam in volcanic ground. Pump water down and up to heat a town and watch the ground around the well cool over years, then rest it and watch the heat creep back; move the well to Iceland or beside a hot spring and compare. A map shows the heat measured flowing out of the ground around the world.
takeaway: The ground gets hotter the deeper you go, so a deep enough well reaches heat that can warm a house or boil water, soonest where volcanoes are near.
needs: Measured heat flow out of the ground around the world, for the map and the local gradient: the IHFC Global Heat Flow Database (CC BY 4.0).
pitfall: Underground heat is not the Sun's heat stored in the ground: the Sun warms only the top few metres, and below that the warmth comes from the Earth itself. Nor is it endless at one spot: pump too fast and the rock around the well cools for decades.
why: US DOE, 'Geothermal basics', https://www.energy.gov/eere/geothermal/geothermal-basics (curriculum: NGSS 4-ESS3-1, energy resources)
overlapWith: plate-tectonics: that page shows where volcanoes are and why; this page follows the heat down a well anywhere, and what pumping it out does to the ground.
needsSource: IHFC Global Heat Flow Database, https://ihfc-iugg.org/products/global-heat-flow-database (CC BY 4.0).

title: Glaciers: rivers of ice
interaction: A mountain valley in cross-section, with snow falling on the high ground and melting on the low ground; press play and the snow that outlasts the summer packs into ice, and the ice, once thick enough, creeps downhill like very slow honey, dragging rocks that scrape the valley into a U. The one control is the climate: make it colder or snowier and the front advances, warmer and the front retreats. Flags frozen into the ice show that the ice itself still flows forward even while the front is retreating.
takeaway: A glacier is a slow river of ice whose front moves forward or back depending on whether the snow it gains up high outpaces the melting at its toe, while the ice itself always flows downhill.
needsSource: none (a one-dimensional shallow-ice flowline with Glen's flow law and a snowfall-minus-melt balance that depends on height; PhET's legacy Glaciers sim is the reference interaction)
pitfall: A retreating glacier does not flow backward or uphill: it melts at its toe faster than it flows forward.
why: England KS3 geography: 'glaciation, hydrology and coasts' (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-geography-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-geography-programmes-of-study); PhET Glaciers (https://phet.colorado.edu/en/simulations/glaciers).
overlapWith: ice-ages (level 2) explains when ice sheets grow from orbital cycles; this page shows how one glacier flows and why its front moves.

title: How caves form
interaction: A block of limestone threaded with hair-thin cracks, and slightly acid rainwater seeping in from the top; press play with the clock running thousands of years. Water flows where it can and dissolves a little rock as it goes, and every crack it widens carries more water and so widens faster, until one path wins and swells into a tunnel while the others stay cracks; the one control is how acid the rain is. Lower the water table and the tunnel drains into an air-filled cave where drips start building stalactites.
takeaway: Caves are dissolved, not dug: the crack that carries the most water widens fastest, so a maze of hair-thin cracks turns into one big tunnel.
needsSource: none (a fracture-network karst model: flow through a crack growing with the cube of its width, dissolution from the standard calcite kinetics, a sped-up clock)
pitfall: Most caves were not washed out by underground rivers or cracked open by earthquakes: the rock was dissolved, slowly, by water that was only slightly acid.
why: England KS3 geography: 'rocks, weathering and soils' (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-geography-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-geography-programmes-of-study); US National Park Service, Caves and Karst (https://www.nps.gov/subjects/caves/index.htm).
overlapWith: acids-bases (level 1) shows acids reacting; this page is about a positive feedback in flow, and the acid is only the thing that does the dissolving.

title: From cloud droplet to raindrop, or hailstone
interaction: A cloud of tiny droplets hangs in gently rising air, each falling slower than the air rises, so the cloud floats; press play and droplets bump and merge, and the bigger one gets the faster it falls and the more it sweeps up, until it outruns the updraft and drops out as rain, a size scale showing the drop is a hundred droplets across and took about a million of them. The one control is the updraft: turn it up and the drops grow larger before they fall, the difference between drizzle and a downpour. Turn it up to thunderstorm strength and the drops are carried above the freezing height, where each trip up adds a layer of ice until a hailstone too heavy for the wind drops out, and you can cut it open and count the rings.
takeaway: A cloud droplet must merge with about a million others before it falls faster than the air that holds the cloud up, so rain is the end of a chain of collisions, and the stronger the rising air, the bigger what finally falls, up to hail.
needsSource: none (collision-coalescence growth with terminal velocities from the standard published fall-speed relation for water drops, and an ice sphere's fall speed against the updraft for the hail step)
pitfall: Raindrops are not tear-shaped: small ones are spheres and big ones flatten into buns. A cloud does not rain because it has become too heavy, and hail is not frozen rain and does not need a cold day: it falls from summer thunderstorms whose tops are far below freezing.
why: NGSS MS-ESS2-4, whose clarification stresses 'the ways water changes its state as it moves through the multiple pathways of the hydrologic cycle' (https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/ms-ess2-4-earths-systems); NGSS 3-ESS3-1 on weather-related hazards (https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/3-ess3-1-earth-and-human-activity).
overlapWith: cloud-base: that page ends where a cloud appears; this one asks why its droplets stay up and what has to happen before they come down.

title: Lighthouses: how far a light can be seen
interaction: Raise a lighthouse's lamp up its tower and watch the lit stretch of sea grow as the Earth's curve stops hiding it; a ship sails in from beyond the horizon and its lookout sees the flash first from the crow's nest, then from the deck. Spin the lamp's lens to send a beam round and set its rhythm of flashes from a real list of lights; the ship reads the rhythm to tell this lighthouse from the next one down the coast.
takeaway: The Earth's curve hides a low light, so lighthouses are tall and lookouts climb high, and each light's rhythm of flashes is its name.
needs: Heights, ranges and flash characteristics of a few named lighthouses from the US Coast Guard Light List (US government work, public domain).
pitfall: A light is not hidden by distance alone: on a flat Earth a bright enough lamp would be seen from anywhere. The lens does not make the lamp brighter; it gathers light that would be wasted upward and sideways into a beam, which is why the light flashes as the beam sweeps past.
why: The US Coast Guard Light List, the real register of lights and their characteristics, https://www.navcen.uscg.gov/light-lists ('how far can you see a lighthouse' is a common search question)
overlapWith: light-optics: that page traces rays through lenses on a bench; this page does not trace the lens at all, it uses the curve of the Earth and the rhythm of flashes.
needsSource: USCG Light List (public domain), https://www.navcen.uscg.gov/light-lists

title: Lightning and thunder: count the seconds
interaction: A storm scene: a charged cloud, open ground and a palette of things to place on it (a tree, a house, a tall rod, a person); press strike and a branching bolt grows down from the cloud step by step, landing on the tallest thing near its path more often than anywhere else. Then the flash reaches the viewer at once while the thunder's sound front crawls out at a third of a kilometre per second, a counter ticking off the seconds until it arrives. Drag the viewer farther away: more seconds, fainter rumble.
takeaway: Thunder is the sound of the lightning you already saw: light arrives at once and sound takes about three seconds per kilometre, so counting the gap tells how far away the storm is, and the bolt favours the tallest path to the ground.
needsSource: none (the dielectric-breakdown model of Niemeyer, Pietronero and Wiesmann, 1984, grown on a grid with grounded objects; sound at 343 m/s)
pitfall: Thunder is not clouds bumping together, and lightning does strike the same place twice: tall things get hit again and again.
why: US National Weather Service, 'Understanding Lightning: Thunder', with the count-the-seconds rule (https://www.weather.gov/safety/lightning-science-thunder); KS2 Year 4 Sound: 'sounds get fainter as the distance from the sound source increases'.
overlapWith: waves-interference (level 1) treats sound as a wave with speed and Doppler shift; this page uses only the fact that sound is slow and light is not, plus where a bolt goes.

title: How rivers carve valleys
interaction: Rain falls on a bumpy block of land shown from above and in cross-section. Water runs downhill, joins into streams, picks up soil where it runs fast and drops it where it slows: the streams branch like a tree, cut valleys, and a fan of dropped mud grows where the river meets the sea. One control: how much it rains; a later step lifts the land to see the rivers cut faster.
takeaway: Rivers do not just follow valleys, they make them: moving water carries the land downhill a grain at a time and drops it wherever it slows.
needsSource: none (a cellular hydraulic-erosion model: flow routing on a small grid, erosion by fast water with a carrying limit, deposition where it slows, hillslope creep; optionally a real hillside from USGS 3DEP elevation, public domain)
pitfall: A valley is not a crack that opened: the river removed what used to fill it, and it took far longer than a lifetime.
why: NGSS 4-ESS2-1: 'Make observations and/or measurements to provide evidence of the effects of weathering or the rate of erosion by water, ice, wind, or vegetation' (https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/4-ess2-1-earths-systems); England KS2 geography, rivers.
overlapWith: plate-tectonics (level 1) builds mountains; this page wears them down, and it is the only page where water shapes the land.

title: Where sand comes from
interaction: Step a chunk of rock down a river: it breaks off a cliff, bangs along in a flood, and at each stop it is rounder and smaller as its corners knock off, faster for soft rock than hard. Where the river slows, the grains it carries settle by size, boulders first, then gravel, then sand, with mud going farthest; at the beach the waves finish the job. Scrub back and forth along the river to see where each size ends up.
takeaway: Every grain of sand on a beach is a piece of a mountain that was knocked smaller and rounder on its way down, and the river sorts the grains by size as it slows.
needsSource: none (Sternberg's law of downstream abrasion with published coefficients for a few rock types, and settling speeds by grain size)
pitfall: Sand is not all ground up by the sea, and not all sand is quartz: white tropical sand is broken shell and coral.
why: England KS2 science, Year 3 Rocks: 'compare and group together different kinds of rocks on the basis of their appearance and simple physical properties' (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study); NGSS 4-ESS2-1.
overlapWith: river-valleys: that page shows the land being cut; this one follows a single rock through the cutting and asks what becomes of it.

title: How dunes march
interaction: A flat bed of sand under a steady wind, drawn as little stacked slabs; press play and the wind lifts grains from the side facing it and drops them a little downwind, they pile until a slope gets too steep and slides, and out of a flat bed grows a field of dunes, each with a gentle face toward the wind and a steep slip face behind. The one control is the wind's direction, later its strength. Turn the wind and the dunes slowly rebuild to face it; everything creeps downwind.
takeaway: Dunes are the wind moving sand uphill one grain at a time and the sand sliding down the back, so a whole dune walks downwind and always faces into the wind.
needsSource: none (Werner's 1995 cellular dune model: sand slabs, wind shadows, avalanching at the angle of repose)
pitfall: Deserts are not defined by sand or by heat but by dryness: most desert is rock and gravel, and some of it is cold.
why: NGSS 4-ESS2-1, erosion by wind (https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/4-ess2-1-earths-systems); US National Park Service, 'Aeolian (Dunes) Landforms' (https://www.nps.gov/subjects/geology/aeolian-landforms.htm).
overlapWith: rock-to-sand makes the grains; this page is what the wind does with them, and no existing page shows a landform built by wind.

title: Where wind comes from: the sea breeze
interaction: A coast in cross-section, land on one side and sea on the other, filled with air drawn as drifting particles. Drag the Sun across the sky: by afternoon the land is warmer than the sea, the air over it rises, and air from the sea slides in underneath as a breeze that a flag on the beach shows. At night the land cools faster than the water and the breeze turns around and blows out to sea.
takeaway: Wind is air moving from where it is cool and heavy toward where it is warm and rising, so uneven heating of land and water is enough to make a wind blow, and to turn it around at night.
needsSource: none (a small 2D buoyant-convection solver on a coarse grid, with the sea slower to warm than the land)
pitfall: Warm air does not rise because heat goes up: it rises because it is lighter than the cooler air around it, which pushes it up.
why: NOAA JetStream, 'The Sea Breeze' (https://www.noaa.gov/jetstream/ocean/sea-breeze); NGSS MS-ESS2-5 on air masses moving from high to low pressure.
overlapWith: atmosphere-weather (level 2) heats a whole spinning globe into convection cells and winds with Coriolis; this page heats one beach and gets one wind, no rotation.

title: Why snowflakes have six arms
interaction: Start from a speck in cold, moist air and watch a crystal grow on a honeycomb grid: water molecules arrive from all sides, the corners that stick out catch more of them, and six arms shoot out and branch. One control: the amount of moisture in the air, then the temperature. Low moisture grows flat plates and stubby prisms, high moisture grows branching stars, and a little randomness means no two crystals come out the same, though every one keeps its six-fold symmetry.
takeaway: Six-fold symmetry comes from the way water molecules pack, and the shape of the arms comes from the air the crystal grew in, so every snowflake is a record of its own journey.
needsSource: none (Reiter's 2005 hexagonal cellular automaton for snow crystal growth, or the Gravner-Griffeath 2008 model, checked against the Nakaya morphology diagram)
pitfall: Snowflakes are not frozen raindrops; that is sleet. A snow crystal grows from vapour straight into ice.
why: NOAA, 'How do snowflakes form? Get the science behind snow' (https://www.noaa.gov/stories/how-do-snowflakes-form-science-behind-snow); KS2 Year 4 states of matter.
overlapWith: states-of-matter (level 1) shows water freezing into its open lattice; this page shows a single crystal growing from vapour and why its shape depends on the air.

title: What soil is made of: the jar test
interaction: Scoop soil from a chosen place (a sandy garden, a clay field, a forest floor, a river bank) into a jar of water, shake it and step the clock: after a minute the sand has dropped to the bottom, after an hour the silt lies on top of it, and a day later the cloudy water has finally let its clay down, while bits of rotted leaf and root still float. A ruler reads the thickness of each layer and names the soil from the mix. A last step pours water on each soil: it runs straight through the sandy one and sits for hours on the clay.
takeaway: Soil is rock ground into grains of three sizes plus the rotted remains of living things, and the mix decides whether water runs through it or stays.
needsSource: none (settling speeds by grain size from Stokes' law, the sand, silt and clay size classes and the USDA soil texture triangle, US Department of Agriculture work, public domain)
pitfall: Soil is not dirt that was always there and is not the same everywhere: a few centimetres take centuries to form, and the floating bits are as much a part of soil as the grains.
why: England KS2 science, Year 3 Rocks: 'recognise that soils are made from rocks and organic matter' (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study); the jar test is a standard extension-service activity (https://hgic.clemson.edu/factsheet/soil-texture-analysis-the-jar-test/).
overlapWith: rock-to-sand: that page sorts grains by size along a river; this one sorts them in a jar the reader can shake at home and adds the half of soil that was never rock.

title: How a tornado spins up
interaction: A wide, slowly turning column of air under a thunderstorm, drawn as rings of particles. Drag the storm's updraft to stretch the column taller and thinner: the particles keep their swing but have less room, so they whirl faster, like a skater pulling in her arms, and a funnel appears where the whirl is fast enough for the pressure drop at its heart to make a cloud. Let the column widen again and it slows and the funnel fades.
takeaway: A spinning column of air spins faster when it is stretched thinner, and the funnel you see is just the place where the whirl is fast enough to make a cloud.
needsSource: none (a Rankine-type vortex with angular momentum conserved under stretching, particle advection, and the pressure drop that condenses the funnel)
pitfall: The visible funnel is not the whole tornado: the wind spins just as hard outside it before the cloud appears, which is why damage starts before the funnel seems to touch down.
why: NGSS 3-ESS3-1, weather-related hazards (https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/3-ess3-1-earth-and-human-activity); 'how do tornadoes form' is a standing how-does-it-work question.
overlapWith: atmosphere-weather (level 2) grows a hurricane from a warm sea on a rotating globe; this page stretches one small vortex with no Coriolis effect at all.

title: Why some volcanoes explode and others ooze
interaction: Step magma up a pipe toward the surface with gas dissolved in it like a shaken fizzy drink: as the weight of rock above lessens, bubbles appear and grow. The one control is how runny or sticky the magma is: runny magma lets the bubbles float out, and lava fountains and flows spill gently down the slope, while sticky magma traps them until the froth bursts and the cone blows its top in ash. A second control adds more gas and makes the sticky case worse.
takeaway: What makes an eruption explosive is not how hot the magma is but how hard it is for its gas to get out: runny magma fizzes, sticky magma bursts.
needsSource: none (bubble growth as pressure falls, bubble rise speed set by the magma's viscosity, fragmentation above a gas fraction threshold)
pitfall: Lava is not fire and a volcano is not a hole into a burning centre: magma is melted rock, and most of the Earth's inside is solid.
why: USGS FAQ, 'How do volcanoes erupt?', runny magma that lets gas escape against sticky magma that traps it (https://www.usgs.gov/faqs/how-do-volcanoes-erupt); England KS2 geography, volcanoes and earthquakes.
overlapWith: plate-tectonics (level 1) shows where volcanoes are and why; this page shows what happens inside one when it erupts, which that page does not.

title: The water cycle
interaction: A sea, a mountain and the sky, with the water drawn as a few hundred dots that the page follows one by one. Turn the Sun up and more dots leave the sea as invisible vapour, rise, cool and gather into clouds that rain on the mountain, from where streams carry them back to the sea; turn it down and the air dries and the rivers shrink. A counter shows how many dots are in the sea, the air, the ice and the rivers at any moment, and the sea always holds almost all of them.
takeaway: Water is never used up: the same water goes round and round between sea, air and land, lifted by the Sun's heat and brought back down by gravity.
needsSource: none (the share of water in each store from the USGS Water Science School, US Government work, public domain)
pitfall: Evaporation does not need boiling: water leaves the sea at ordinary temperatures, faster when it is warmer. And the vapour is invisible; the white of a cloud is droplets.
why: England KS2 science, Year 4 States of matter: 'identify the part played by evaporation and condensation in the water cycle' and 'associate the rate of evaporation with temperature' (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study); also NGSS MS-ESS2-4 (https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/ms-ess2-4-earths-systems).
overlapWith: carbon-cycle: the same idea of stores joined by flows, but for water, with every drop followed as a particle in a landscape instead of flows drawn to scale between boxes.

title: Why the sea is salty
interaction: A lake fed by a river that carries a pinch of salt in every bucket of water; the Sun lifts pure water out and the salt stays. Open or close the lake's outlet: with an outlet the salt leaves as fast as it arrives and the lake stays fresh, close it and the salt count climbs year after year until crystals ring the shore, like the Dead Sea. Then the ocean: rivers in, evaporation out, and salt also leaving into the sea floor, so its saltiness holds steady at about two teaspoons of salt in every glass.
takeaway: Rivers carry a little salt to the sea and the Sun takes only the water back, so salt collects wherever water can leave only by evaporating.
needsSource: none (a salt mass-balance box model; seawater at about 35 g per kg and the average river at about 0.1 g per litre, from the USGS Water Science School, US Government work)
pitfall: The ocean is not getting steadily saltier today: salt leaves into the sea floor about as fast as rivers bring it.
why: USGS Water Science School, 'Why is the ocean salty?' (https://www.usgs.gov/special-topics/water-science-school/science/why-ocean-salty); 'why is the sea salty?' is among the questions UK parents say they cannot answer (https://www.stornowaygazette.co.uk/arts-and-culture/top-30-impossible-questions-that-children-ask-840687).
overlapWith: ocean-currents (level 2) uses salinity to drive the deep circulation; this page asks where the salt came from and never mentions currents.

title: Auroras: the Sun's wind on Earth's magnet
interaction: Earth with its magnetic field drawn as loops, in a stream of charged specks from the Sun; press play and the specks cannot cross the field lines, so they slide along them and spiral down into the air in two rings around the magnetic poles, where the sky glows green and, higher up, red. The one control is the strength of the solar wind. A gust squeezes the field and the glowing rings widen toward the equator, which is when people far from the poles get to see the lights.
takeaway: Auroras happen in rings around the magnetic poles because Earth's magnetic field steers the Sun's charged particles there, and a stronger solar wind pushes the rings toward the equator.
needsSource: none (charged particles integrated in a dipole field, the field's sunward edge pushed in by solar-wind pressure, glow colour by height; the page states the simplification that particles are shown guided straight down the field lines, where the real ones arrive by way of the night-side tail; the NOAA SWPC OVATION aurora forecast, public domain, can be shown for comparison)
pitfall: Auroras are not sunlight reflected off polar ice, and they are not in the clouds: they glow a hundred kilometres up and higher.
why: NASA Space Place, 'What Is an Aurora?' (https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/aurora/en/).
overlapWith: electromagnetism (level 2) shows charges moving in fields in the abstract; this page shows it once, on a planet, with the pattern it makes in the sky.

title: Comets and their tails
interaction: Scrub a comet along its real stretched orbit, far out and frozen, then swinging in close to the Sun. As it warms, gas and dust stream off it, and the tail always points away from the Sun, whichever way the comet is going, so on the way out the comet flies tail-first. Two tails appear: a straight blue gas tail pushed by the solar wind and a curved dust tail of grains that lag along the orbit; zoom in to see the grains leave.
takeaway: A comet's tail is blown by the Sun, not left behind by motion, so it always points away from the Sun and the comet travels tail-first when it leaves.
needs: Orbital elements of one or two real comets (Halley, and a recent bright one) from the JPL Small-Body Database API (https://ssd-api.jpl.nasa.gov/doc/sbdb.html); NASA/JPL data with no separate licence text, free to use with the credit 'Courtesy NASA/JPL-Caltech' under JPL's use policy. Treat as open but confirm against the API's terms before shipping.
needsSource: JPL Small-Body Database orbital elements (NASA/JPL, free with credit; no explicit data licence)
pitfall: The tail does not trail behind like exhaust, and a comet is not a burning rock: it is ice and dust turning to gas in sunlight.
why: NASA Space Place, 'What Is a Comet?' (https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/comets/en/); England KS2 Year 5, the movement of bodies relative to the Sun.
overlapWith: orbits-kepler (level 1) launches bodies into ellipses; this page uses one real ellipse and asks only which way the tail points.

title: Why the sky is dark at night
interaction: Stand in a forest drawn from above and widen it: with a few trees you see out between the trunks, but keep adding trees farther away and every line of sight ends on bark, so the forest closes into a wall. Then swap trees for stars scattered through space at their real sparseness and press play: light from the stars has been travelling only as long as the universe has existed, so only the stars within that distance can be seen, and a counter shows the sky is still almost entirely black. Drag the age of the universe up and watch the sky slowly fill; it would take an unimaginably longer time than the real one before the night sky glowed like the Sun's surface everywhere.
takeaway: In an endless forest of stars shining forever, every direction would end on a star and the night sky would blaze; it is dark because the universe has an age, so the light from most of those stars has not arrived yet.
needsSource: none (the fraction of the sky covered by stars of a given size scattered at a given density out to the light-travel distance, computed by counting lines of sight; the page states the simplification that it ignores the stretching of light by the expansion of space, which darkens the sky further)
pitfall: The sky is not dark because stars are too far or too faint, or because dust hides them: with endless stars for endless time the faint ones would add up and the dust would glow too. It is dark because light has had only a limited time to travel.
why: Olbers' paradox is a standing popular question: Scientific American, 'Why Is the Sky Dark at Night? You Can Thank the Big Bang' (https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/why-is-the-night-sky-dark-olbers); the MinutePhysics video 'Why is it dark at night?' (https://www.universetoday.com/97678/video-why-is-the-sky-dark-at-night).
overlapWith: big-bang (level 2) runs the expansion and the timeline of the universe; this page uses only one consequence of the universe having an age, that light has had limited time to travel, and never mentions expansion on the stage.

title: Earth is a ball
interaction: Drag a ship out to sea and watch it from the shore: on a flat world it only shrinks, but on the round one its hull disappears before its sails as the sea bulges up between you and it, and climbing a cliff brings it back into view. Then walk a little figure around the globe: wherever it stands its feet point to the middle, and a dropped ball falls toward the middle too, so nobody on the far side falls off.
takeaway: The world is a ball, so the sea itself hides the bottom of a distant ship, and 'down' means toward the middle wherever you stand.
needsSource: none (the geometry of a sphere: horizon distance from eye height and the height hidden beyond it; gravity drawn toward the centre)
pitfall: People on the far side are not upside down and do not have to hold on: the page draws no up arrow anywhere. And the ship does not vanish because it got too small.
why: NGSS 5-PS2-1: 'Support an argument that the gravitational force exerted by Earth on objects is directed down', with 'down' pointing toward the center of the spherical Earth (https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/5-ps2-1-motion-and-stability-forces-and-interactions); England KS2 Year 5: 'describe the sun, Earth and moon as approximately spherical bodies'.
overlapWith: sun-earth-moon (level 1) tilts and orbits the Earth; this page never moves it, only shows that it is round and which way down is.

title: Rockets: going up by throwing things down
interaction: Stand on a skateboard and throw a ball: you roll the other way, and the harder or heavier the throw the faster you roll; throw a bag of balls one after another and you keep speeding up. Then pump up a bottle rocket on the lawn: water is thrown out of the neck and the bottle shoots up, and sliding the water fill from empty to full finds the amount that goes highest. Launch the same rocket in a vacuum chamber and on the Moon and it still goes.

overlapWith: sorting (level 1) steps bubble, insertion, merge and quick sort one comparison at a time and plots Big-O; this page is a fixed, parallel board of swaps the reader builds and verifies, with no growth curves.
needsSource: none

title: Sound as a list of numbers
interaction: Record a clap or a word (or pick a shipped clip) and see it as a wiggly line; a slider sets how many times a second the computer measures the line, from tens of thousands down to a few hundred, and the measurements appear as dots that join into a new line. Play the dots back: the sound stays itself until the dots get too sparse, then the high parts go first and voices turn muffled and wrong. A second slider sets how many different heights a measurement may take, from thousands down to four, and the sound turns grainy.
takeaway: A recording is a long list of measurements of the air's push taken thousands of times a second, and the sound survives as long as the measurements are frequent and fine enough.

needsSource: none beyond a CC0 clip; sampling and requantising are computed on the page.
pitfall: More measurements per second do not make a sound louder or longer, only truer; the wiggly line is a graph of pressure against time, not a picture of air moving sideways. Do not invoke the sampling theorem by name; show the point where the dots fail.

overlapWith: compression (level 2) uses frequency content to drop detail and fourier-transform decomposes signals; this page stops at measurements, how often and how finely, listened to.

title: Traffic lights that know you are there
interaction: Cars arrive at a crossroads from four directions while a timer runs the lights through a fixed cycle; queues grow on the busy road while the empty road gets its green anyway. Bury a sensor loop in each lane and switch the controller to 'skip a green nobody is waiting for': the queues shrink. Then set the busy road's green longer and shorter and find which choice keeps the total queue smallest.
takeaway: A traffic light is a small counting program, and giving it a sensor so that it can skip empty roads makes the whole crossroads wait less.
needsSource: none; cars arrive at random at set rates and queue, and the loop detector follows the published inductive-loop principle (a metal mass above the loop lowers its inductance and trips the controller).
pitfall: The loop in the road is not a pressure plate: it senses metal, which is why a bicycle may fail to trigger it. Pressing a pedestrian button again does not shorten the wait; the request is registered once.
why: England KS2 computing: 'design, write and debug programs that accomplish specific goals, including controlling or simulating physical systems' (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-computing-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-computing-programmes-of-study); traffic lights are the standard project of the Teach Computing Year 5 physical-computing unit (https://teachcomputing.org/curriculum/key-stage-2/programming-a-selection-in-physical-computing/connecting-crumbles).
overlapWith: feedback-control (level 2) tunes a continuous controller; this one is a rule with a sensor and a timer, with a queue of cars as the cost. graph-search routes one car across a map; this page runs one crossing.

title: Twenty questions: halving the haystack
interaction: Think of a number from 1 to 100 and answer the page's 'higher or lower' questions: a bar of candidates shrinks by half each answer and the counter stops at seven. Now find a word in a thousand-page dictionary by opening it in the middle, then in the middle of the right half, counting the opens, against a search that flips through every page. Then play animal twenty questions: each yes/no question hides half of the hundred animals on the board until one is left.
takeaway: A question that splits what is left in half finds the answer in a handful of steps, where checking one at a time takes hundreds.

title: Barcodes at the checkout
interaction: Drag a scanner's red line across a barcode and watch what it sees, a trace of dark and light over time, then step through it: a start mark, six groups of stripes, a middle mark, six more and an end mark, each group of four widths one digit. Scan slowly, fast, at an angle or upside down and the widths all stretch together, so the digits come out the same. Smudge one stripe and the last digit, a check digit, says the number is wrong.
takeaway: A barcode is a number written as stripe widths, read as proportions so that speed and angle do not matter, with a last digit that catches a misread; the price is looked up afterwards.
needsSource: none; the EAN-13 layout (95 modules, 7 per digit, L/G/R patterns, weighted check digit) from the published GS1 specification.
pitfall: The barcode does not contain the price or the product name; it is a number the till looks up. The scanner reads ratios of widths, not absolute sizes, which is why the code can be printed at any size.

overlapWith: qr-codes in this batch: the two-dimensional cousin with error correction; this page is one row of widths, a check digit and no repair. binary reads bits; here a digit is a pattern of four widths.

title: How your phone finds a tower
interaction: Drag a phone across a town map dotted with towers; each tower's reach is drawn as a fading patch, the bars on the phone follow the nearest strong tower, and a line shows which tower the phone is talking to. Start a call and walk a route: as one tower fades and the next grows, the line jumps over without the call dropping. Drive into a valley or a thick building and watch the bars fall; put a stadium crowd in one patch and watch its calls queue because the tower has only so many lines.

needsSource: none; signal strength from a standard distance-and-obstacle path-loss model, handover to the stronger tower with a margin, and a fixed number of channels per tower. Real tower positions could come from OpenCelliD (CC BY-SA 4.0) but are not needed.
pitfall: Ordinary phones do not talk to satellites, and a text does not go phone to phone: it goes to a tower, into the network and out of another tower. Bars measure the link to the tower, not the distance to the person you are calling.
why: England KS2 computing: 'understand computer networks, including the internet; how they can provide multiple services' (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-computing-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-computing-programmes-of-study); 'Cellular network' averaged about 12,400 views a month on English Wikipedia in 2025.

title: How a password gets guessed
interaction: Type a password (or pick one) and release a guessing machine against it. It tries the hundred thousand most common passwords first and finds '123456' or 'liverpool1' in a blink, then starts counting through every combination: a counter shows how many guesses are left and how long that takes at a million guesses a second. Make the password one letter longer and the count multiplies; swap letters for symbols and it barely moves; type three unrelated words and the counter runs off the chart.
takeaway: Each extra character multiplies the guesses needed, so a long password of ordinary words beats a short one full of symbols, unless it is on the list of common ones that every guesser tries first.
needs: The NCSC and Have I Been Pwned list of the 100,000 most common breached passwords (2019): the NCSC pages quote the top counts but state no licence for the file (NCSC content is usually under the Open Government Licence v3; unconfirmed). Fallback: the top entries and counts quoted in the NCSC announcement plus a permissively licensed word list (SCOWL).
needsSource: NCSC top-100k password list, licence unconfirmed; the counting model itself needs no data.
pitfall: Guessing at the login screen is slow and gets locked out; the fast guessing happens against stolen scrambled copies, which is why strength still matters. Symbol substitutions such as 'p@ssw0rd' are on the lists. The count assumes the guesser does not know your recipe: real guessers also try combinations of common words, so the words must be genuinely unrelated, and the page should say so. Do not show the scrambling itself; hashing is cryptography, level 2.

overlapWith: cryptography (level 2) hashes and signs, and primes-modular-arithmetic shows easy-forward, hard-back; this page is only counting guesses, with the common-password list as the twist.

title: QR codes
interaction: Type a short message and watch it become a square of black and white cells, built the real way: the three big corner squares that tell a camera where the code is and which way up, then the message as cells, then spare cells computed from the message. Point a drawn camera at it from any angle and it reads. Now paint over cells with a brush: the message still comes out, and a counter shows how many cells are damaged; keep painting and find the moment it fails, then paint over a corner square instead, which fails at once.
takeaway: A QR code carries its message plus spare cells computed from it, so a scratched or half-covered code still reads, until too much is gone or the corner finders are hidden.
needs: None to ship; the page runs a real encoder and decoder (open-source implementations of the QR standard exist under MIT and Apache 2.0, e.g. qrcode-generator and jsQR).
needsSource: none; an in-browser QR encoder and decoder (Reed-Solomon) under MIT/Apache 2.0.
