title: Tuning a radio
interaction: Several stations broadcast at once and the antenna wire picks up all of them as one tangled wiggle. Turn the tuning knob: a swing inside the radio that likes one rhythm builds up only for the station whose rhythm matches, and the others fall away; between stations the swing stays small and you hear hiss. Then look at one station's wave up close: the music rides on it as changes in height (AM) or in rhythm (FM); pick which and hear why FM survives a lightning crackle better.
takeaway: Every station reaches the antenna at the same time, and tuning means choosing which rhythm the radio swings along with.
needsSource: none; a sum of carrier waves through a tuned resonant filter whose centre follows the knob, then envelope or frequency detection, synthesised to audio.
pitfall: Radio waves are not sound waves: nothing in the air is playing the music, and the station is not caught alone; selection happens inside the set by resonance. Tuning does not make the other stations leave the wire.
why: 'Radio' averaged about 25,200 views a month on English Wikipedia in 2025 (https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/metrics/pageviews/per-article/en.wikipedia/all-access/user/Radio/monthly/2025010100/2025123100).
overlapWith: oscillations-resonance (level 1) shows one oscillator building up when pushed at its natural frequency, and wireless-signals (level 2) shows modulation; what is new here is many stations on one wire at once and selection by the swing, with sound as the output.

title: What a remote control says
interaction: Press a button on a drawn remote and a lamp on its nose blinks in invisible light; the page shows the blinks slowed a thousand times: a long opening flash, then a string of short flashes with short and long gaps that spell the button's number, then the same string inverted as a check. Hold the button and a short 'still pressed' pattern repeats. Point the remote at the wall and the blinks bounce to the TV; put a hand in front and nothing arrives; look through a phone camera (a front camera especially; many rear ones filter infrared out) and the blinks become visible.
takeaway: A remote talks in fast blinks of invisible light, each button its own pattern of long and short gaps, which is why it needs a clear line, or a wall to bounce off, and many phone cameras can see it.
needsSource: none; the pattern follows the widely documented NEC infrared protocol (38 kHz carrier, 9 ms leader, short and long gaps for 0 and 1, inverted copy of the command, repeat code), with brightness falling with distance and reflection.
pitfall: The remote is not sending heat rays or radio: most TV remotes use infrared light pulses (some newer ones use radio and work through walls; say so). The TV does not see steady light: it listens for flashes at one fast rhythm, which is why sunlight does not change the channel.
why: NGSS 4-PS4-3: 'generate and compare multiple solutions that use patterns to transfer information' (https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/4-ps4-3-waves-and-their-applications-technologies-information-transfer).
overlapWith: wireless-signals (level 2) modulates a carrier and binary reads bits; this page is the everyday object, with the pattern shown as long and short gaps and a line-of-sight model.

title: Wi-Fi around the house
interaction: Place a router on a floor plan and the rooms fill with a signal map; drag the laptop around and its speed gauge follows the colour. Add walls, a brick one, a fridge, a fish tank, and watch each cut a shadow in the map and the gauge drop, as the link slows down to be heard through the loss. Switch the router to the faster, shorter-reach band and compare; then add a neighbour's router on the same channel and watch the two take turns.
takeaway: Wi-Fi is radio: walls and water eat it, the link slows down rather than breaking as the signal fades, and two networks on one channel must take turns.
needsSource: none beyond published indoor loss figures (ITU-R P.1238 indoor propagation model and typical wall losses).
pitfall: Wi-Fi is not the internet; a full signal to the router says nothing about the line out of the house. Distance does not reduce the router's 'speed': the devices slow their sending so that the weaker signal can still be read.
why: NGSS MS-PS4-2: 'waves are reflected, absorbed, or transmitted through various materials' (https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/ms-ps4-2-waves-and-their-applications-technologies-information-transfer); 'Wi-Fi' averaged about 73,900 views a month on English Wikipedia in 2025 (https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/metrics/pageviews/per-article/en.wikipedia/all-access/user/Wi-Fi/monthly/2025010100/2025123100).
overlapWith: wireless-signals (level 2): that page packs bits onto a carrier against noise; this one is where to put the router, computed from a wall-by-wall loss model, with speed shown as a gauge and no waveform.

title: How your phone guesses your word
interaction: Type a word with a slip in it and watch the phone's two counts: which real words are one or two changes away, and how often each of those is used in a huge pile of books. The suggestion is the common one that is close; type a rare name and watch it 'corrected' into a common word. Then type the start of a sentence and see the next-word guesses, which are nothing but a count of which word most often followed the last one in the pile; change the last word and the counts change.
takeaway: A phone guesses your word by counting: which real words are nearest to what you typed and which are used most, so it is confidently wrong whenever you are unusual.
needs: Word and word-pair counts: a subset of the Google Books Ngram data (1-grams and 2-grams, CC BY 3.0, https://storage.googleapis.com/books/ngrams/books/datasetsv3.html), or counts the page builds itself from a Project Gutenberg text (public domain).
needsSource: Google Books Ngram (CC BY 3.0) and/or a public-domain book; Norvig's count_1w and count_2w files derive from the Google Web Trillion Word corpus with no stated data terms, so not those.

overlapWith: language-models (level 2): that page shows a real network's next-token probabilities and sampling; this one has no network, only edit distance and counted word pairs, and the suggestions can be checked by hand.

title: Why a photo cannot unlock your phone
interaction: Turn a head in front of a drawn phone: the phone sprays a pattern of thousands of invisible dots onto it, a second camera sees where each dot lands, and the page shows the depth map they measure, nose nearest, ears farthest. Enrol the head, then present it again turned, smiling or with glasses: the map differs a little and the match bar stays above the line. Hold up a flat photo of the same face and every dot lands at the same depth, so the bar collapses; present a twin's head with the same shape and the bar stays up.
takeaway: Face unlock measures the shape of your face in depth from where a pattern of dots lands, so a flat photo fails while a face with the same shape, a twin, can pass.
needs: A head to measure: a simple parametric head drawn on the page (no external data), or a scanned head if one under an open licence is confirmed.
needsSource: none; depth is computed by triangulating projected dots against the head's surface on the page.
pitfall: It is not reading your eyes or your DNA, and a match is a score above a line, never certainty; the phone follows gradual changes such as a beard by updating the stored map. Name the depth method as one kind (structured light) and say that other phones use other depth tricks.
why: AI4K12 Big Idea 1, Perception (https://ai4k12.org/); 'Face ID' averaged about 14,500 views a month on English Wikipedia in 2025 (https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/metrics/pageviews/per-article/en.wikipedia/all-access/user/Face_ID/monthly/2025010100/2025123100).
overlapWith: fingerprint-match in this batch: the same enough-points-agree rule on ridges; light-optics (level 1) has the ray model. medical-imaging reconstructs a slice from many shadows; here depth comes from where projected dots land.

title: How a phone knows your finger
interaction: Press a finger on a drawn sensor and see what it sees: a small patch of ridges, not the whole print, with the ridge ends and forks marked as dots, which are all the phone keeps. Press again, sliding and turning the finger or pressing only a corner, and watch the match count, how many dots line up, rise or fall past the 'enough' line. Wet the finger or put a cut across it and lose a few dots; press a different finger and watch almost none line up.
takeaway: A phone stores a map of where your ridges end and fork, not a picture, and unlocks when enough of those points line up, never all of them.
needs: Fingerprint images generated on the page with a published synthetic-fingerprint model (an orientation field with cores and deltas filtered into ridges, as in SFinGe, Cappelli et al. 2000), stated on the page as synthetic; the FVC benchmark databases are research-use only and are not shipped.
needsSource: none shipped; synthetic ridges from a published model, with the minutiae extracted by thinning. Real fingerprint databases (FVC, NIST SD) are not openly licensed.

why: AI4K12 Big Idea 1, Perception (https://ai4k12.org/); 'Fingerprint' averaged about 17,700 views a month on English Wikipedia in 2025 (https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/metrics/pageviews/per-article/en.wikipedia/all-access/user/Fingerprint/monthly/2025010100/2025123100).
overlapWith: face-unlock-depth in this batch: the same decision rule, enough points agree, on a different measurement; cryptography (level 2) is how the secret is kept. Nothing existing shows a biometric match.

title: How a spam filter decides
interaction: A pile of real text messages arrives, each already marked spam or not; pick any word, 'free', 'win', 'tonight', 'mum', and see two counts, how many spam messages contain it and how many ordinary ones. Build the filter by letting it count every word, then write a message of your own and watch the words vote: each nudges the score toward spam or not according to its two counts. Try to sneak past with 'fr33' and watch the vote change; mark your message and see the counts update.
takeaway: A spam filter has no idea what a message means: it counts which words turned up more in past spam, which is why spammers misspell and why your 'report spam' clicks teach it.
needs: The SMS Spam Collection (Almeida and Hidalgo, UCI Machine Learning Repository, 5,574 messages, CC BY 4.0), or a subset.
needsSource: UCI SMS Spam Collection, CC BY 4.0 (https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/228/sms+spam+collection).
pitfall: No word is bad: 'free' is only commoner in spam. The filter can be fooled both ways, and how much spam exists overall matters, so a rare kind of message needs stronger evidence; keep that as counts, not Bayes' formula.
why: AI4K12 Big Idea 3, Learning, in the AAAI/CSTA K-12 AI guidelines (https://ai4k12.org/).
overlapWith: bayes-theorem (level 1) counts true and false positives in a grid of 1,000 people and learning-from-data fits a curve; this page builds the simplest real classifier on a real corpus, with word counts the reader can check.

title: How a phone counts your steps
interaction: Play a real recording from a phone on someone's waist as they walk, climb stairs, sit and stand, with the stretches labelled: a line jiggles with every stride. Set the 'that was a step' line and watch the counter: too low and the fidgets during the sitting stretches count as steps, too high and the gentle strolling stretches are missed. Then shake the phone in a drawn car on a bumpy road and watch the counter climb without anyone walking.
takeaway: A step counter counts jolts of a shaking sensor, so it needs a line between a stride and a fidget, and a bumpy ride can count as a walk.

It labels activity stretches but records no step counts, so there is no step ground truth: false counts are steps counted while sitting or standing, and the walking count is judged against the strides visible in the trace. The bumpy-car trace is synthesised and said to be.

why: AI4K12 Big Idea 1, Perception: 'computers perceive the world using sensors' (https://ai4k12.org/); 'Pedometer' averaged about 3,800 views a month on English Wikipedia in 2025.
overlapWith: newtons-laws (level 1) is forces and motion and feedback-control reads sensors into a controller; nothing existing counts events in a real sensor trace.

title: Teach a machine to tell things apart
interaction: Draw a few cats and a few houses (or pull examples from a pile of other people's doodles), label them, and draw a new one: the machine shrinks every drawing to a small grid of squares, finds the stored drawings most like the new one square by square, and the labels of those neighbours vote. Watch it get the first guesses wrong, add more examples and watch the votes firm up. Then teach it a trap: every cat drawn in the top corner, every house at the bottom, and see it decide by position instead of shape.
takeaway: A machine learns to sort things by comparing new examples with the ones it was shown, so more and more varied examples make it better, and a lazy pattern in the examples teaches it the wrong thing.

title: How a speaker hears its name

Whisper, add kitchen noise or say a word it never learned, and watch the bars fall or the 'unknown' bar rise. The page says which words the network knows and that everything after the wake word goes to a bigger computer.

title: Why the app says 'you might also like'

Then add a brand-new page with no visits and see that nothing can recommend it yet.

title: A solar panel through the day
interaction: Tilt and turn a solar panel on a roof while the sun crosses the sky for the chosen date and place; a meter shows the panel's output, biggest when it faces the sun squarely and zero at night. Scrub the year: a panel set for summer loses out in winter, and a cloud passing over cuts the meter at once. Compare a flat panel, a tilted one and one that follows the sun as counts of homes lit over a year.
takeaway: A solar panel makes most when it faces the sun squarely, so its tilt, the hour, the season and the clouds all show up in its output.
pitfall: A panel needs light, not heat: it makes less on a hot day, not more, and a cold bright winter noon beats a hot hazy afternoon. The sun is not overhead at noon outside the tropics, so a flat panel is never the best one.
why: NGSS 4-ESS3-1, energy from renewable resources, https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/4-ess3-1-earth-and-human-activity ('which way should solar panels face' is a common search question)

title: Toilet flush & siphons
interaction: Press the lever: the flapper lifts, the tank pours into the bowl and the bowl's water climbs toward the top of the bend behind it. The moment it spills over, the whole bend fills and the bowl drains itself, fast, until air gets in and it gurgles to a stop. Then pour a bucket in slowly or quickly to find what starts the siphon, and watch the float rise with the refilling tank and shut its own valve.
takeaway: The tank does not push anything down the drain; it only raises the bowl high enough to fill the bend, and from then on the siphon empties the bowl by itself until air breaks it.
pitfall: The flush is not a pump and not 'suction': the bowl drains because the water in the falling leg of the bend outweighs the water in the rising leg, and a slow pour that never fills the bend drains nothing.

overlapWith: feedback-control: that page tunes PID gains on a pendulum, a drone and a car at level 2; here the float valve is only the last step, an on/off switch, and the page is the siphon, which no existing page shows.

title: Umbrella
interaction: Slide the runner up the shaft and watch the short stretchers push the ribs outward until the canopy is taut and the runner clicks into its catch; slide it down and the ribs fold in. Then blow wind at the open umbrella from below with a slider: the ribs bend, and past a gust strength the canopy flips inside out, which a second slider for rib stiffness delays.
takeaway: An umbrella opens because a sliding ring pushes short struts that lever the ribs outward, and it flips inside out when wind from below pushes the ribs past the point where they can push back.
pitfall: Wind does not pull the umbrella up: air from below pushes on the canopy, and it is the catch that holds the runner, not the ribs, that keeps it open.
why: KS2 design and technology, mechanical systems including levers and linkages (STEM Learning KS2 'Mechanical systems' collection, https://stem.org.uk/node/466480; statutory text in the primary national curriculum, https://dera.ioe.ac.uk/18300/1/PRIMARY_national_curriculum.pdf).
overlapWith: flight: that page is lift on a wing with streamlines and a pressure map at level 2; here the wind is only a load on a linkage the reader opens and closes with a runner.

title: Vacuum cleaner
interaction: Switch on the fan and watch it push air out of the body, so the air inside thins and the room's air pushes in through the nozzle, carrying dust grains along wherever the airflow past them is strong enough to lift them. Narrow the nozzle, lift it off the carpet, or let the bag fill with dust and watch the airflow and the lifting change; block the hose and the fan roars while nothing moves.
takeaway: A vacuum cleaner does not pull: its fan empties the air inside, the room's air rushes in to fill the gap and carries the dust, and if the flow is blocked the fan can roar without lifting anything.
pitfall: Suction is not a pull and more motor power is not more cleaning: a full bag or a blocked hose defeats the strongest fan, because it is the airflow that carries the dust.
why: KS3 science, Year 8 pressure in fluids: gas pressure and atmospheric pressure as the push of air (scheme at https://flipeducation.ai/curriculum/gb/science/year-8/pressure-in-fluids); nearest standard, no page-specific signal was found before the search budget ran out.
overlapWith: atmosphere-weather: that page lets pressure differences drive wind and weather over a map at level 2; here the pressure difference is made by a fan in a box and the wind is in a hose.
needsSource: none

title: Taps, pipes & water towers
interaction: Fill a water tower, lay pipes from it to a house and open a tap: a gauge shows the push of the water growing with the tower's height, and the flow from the tap growing with that push and shrinking as the pipe gets longer or thinner. Open a second tap, run the shower upstairs and downstairs at once, or kink the garden hose, and watch the flows share out; raise the tower to fix a feeble upstairs shower.
takeaway: What pushes water out of a tap is the height of the water above it, and every long or thin pipe on the way uses up part of that push, which is why the upstairs shower weakens when a downstairs tap opens.
pitfall: A pump does not push water straight to each tap, and opening a tap wider does not raise the pressure: it lowers it, because more flow loses more push in the pipes.
why: KS3 physics, pressure in liquids set by depth, with the pipe network as the familiar case (end points at https://files.schudio.com/oswaldtwistleschool/files/documents/KS3_Physics_End_Points.pdf; Year 8 scheme at https://flipeducation.ai/curriculum/gb/science/year-8/pressure-in-fluids).

needsSource: none

title: Wind turbines: a little more wind, a lot more power
interaction: Turn up the wind over a turbine and watch the blades spin faster while a row of houses lights up one by one; the count of lit houses climbs far faster than the wind does, and doubling the wind lights eight times as many. Lengthen the blades for more, then push the wind past the turbine's limit and watch it hold steady and finally feather its blades and stop. A real wind farm's measured power against wind speed is drawn under the toy's curve.
takeaway: Doubling the wind speed gives a turbine about eight times the power, so where a turbine stands matters more than how big it is.
needs: Measured ten-minute power and wind-speed records of a real wind farm as the reference curve: the Kelmarsh or Penmanshiel SCADA data on Zenodo (Cubico Sustainable Investments, CC BY 4.0).
pitfall: More wind is not always more power: above its rated wind the turbine holds its output steady, and above cut-out it stops, so the eight-times rule holds only below rated power. The blades turn because the wind lifts them like a wing, not because it pushes them from behind.
why: NGSS 4-ESS3-1, obtaining energy from natural resources, and the US DOE's much-visited 'How do wind turbines work' explainer: https://www.energy.gov/eere/wind/how-do-wind-turbines-work
overlapWith: power-grid: that page dispatches wind as one source among many to hold the grid's frequency; this page is one turbine, the wind alone, and the cube law shown as a count of lit houses.
needsSource: Kelmarsh (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5841834) and Penmanshiel (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5946808) wind farm SCADA datasets, CC BY 4.0.

title: Wind-up toys
interaction: Turn the key of a toy and watch its spiral spring coil tighter, with a counter of turns stored; let go and the spring unwinds through a train of gears into the legs, and the toy walks until the counter reaches zero. Swap the gear train for a faster or a slower one and see the toy run quickly for a short time or slowly for a long time from the same turns; add a spinning fan governor and watch it even out the speed.
takeaway: Every turn you put into the spring comes back out through the gears, so a gear train that makes the toy slower makes it walk for longer, because the stored turns are all you have to spend.
pitfall: Winding faster stores nothing extra, and the spring does not run out all at once: its push weakens as it unwinds, which is why the toy slows at the end unless a governor evens it out.
why: KS2 design and technology: pupils 'understand and use mechanical systems in their products, for example gears, pulleys, cams, levers and linkages' (primary national curriculum, https://dera.ioe.ac.uk/18300/1/PRIMARY_national_curriculum.pdf; teaching collection at https://planbee.com/collections/mechanisms-mechanical-systems).
overlapWith: newtons-laws: that page shows energy bars on a track; here energy is stored as counted turns in a spring and spent through a gear train, which no existing page shows.
needsSource: none

title: Zipper
interaction: Drag the slider up and watch its Y-shaped channel bend the two tapes toward each other so that each tooth's hook drops into the hollow between the two teeth across from it; drag it down and the wedge inside prises them apart one at a time. Then pull the two sides of a closed stretch apart with a growing force and see every locked tooth take a share of it, and pull the same way on an open stretch.
takeaway: A zip holds because each tooth is trapped by the two teeth across from it, and only the slider's wedge can free them, one at a time.
pitfall: The slider does not stick or lock the teeth: it only bends the tapes so the staggered teeth can interleave, and once interleaved they hold each other.
why: 'How Zippers Work' is a long-running HowStuffWorks everyday-innovations explainer (https://science.howstuffworks.com/innovation/everyday-innovations/zipper.htm/printable).
overlapWith: bridges-structures: that page loads a structure the reader built and colours members by tension and compression; a zip is a chain of identical hooks that the slider engages and frees one by one, and the pull test only shows that the chain shares a load.
